title: Dearer than oneself
hookLine: King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika agree no one is dearer than oneself; so harm no other

lines: A TENDER QUESTION, AND A TEST.
cards: A palace roof, a husband and a wife, and a question that's half tender and half a test. King Pasenadi of Kosala, whom you've met kissing the Buddha's feet, is on the upper terrace of his palace with Queen Mallika.
And he asks her: Mallika, is there anyone dearer to you than yourself? It's not hard to imagine what answer a husband might hope for. The text doesn't say what he hoped.

teach.b: No, your majesty, Mallika says. There is no one dearer to me than myself. And is there anyone dearer to you than yourself?

The king thinks, and says: no, Mallika, for me too, there is no one dearer than myself. It's a startlingly honest exchange between a husband and a wife. Pasenadi goes down from the palace and tells the Buddha.
And the Buddha, knowing the meaning of this, speaks the verse. Searching all directions with the mind, one finds no one anywhere dearer than oneself.
In the same way, each person holds themselves dear.
So one who loves himself should not harm another. Look at what just happened. Something that sounds selfish, I love myself most, turns in two lines into the ground of kindness.
The verse takes their honesty and turns it outward: if it's true for me, it's true for everyone.
The week behind: Upasiva's crossing, the Udana opening, doubts vanishing under the tree, Bahiya in the street and no time to lose, the boys at the pond, and now the palace roof.
Yesterday the logic of pain, today the logic of love: the same step from me to you.

how: Teachers of metta, loving-kindness, often begin with goodwill toward oneself and then extend the same wish to others, and some cite the verse to Pasenadi and Mallika as the reason.

o: loyal, devoted to a king or master
proud, thinking too highly of yourself
dear, beloved, held close to the heart

games.q: dearer than oneself: tap the pairs.
p: no one is dearer to me than myself
for me too, no one dearer

s: Mallika told the king he was dearer to her than herself
she said no one was dearer to her than herself, and he said the same.
Pasenadi went to the Buddha and told him about the conversation
he went down from the palace, told the Buddha, and the Buddha spoke the verse.
the verse says each person holds themselves dear
searching every direction, no one is dearer than oneself, and so it is for others.

games.q: you're the Buddha. a king tells you that he and his queen each love themselves more than anyone. what do you say?
o: since everyone holds themselves this dear, harm no one.
games.why: he doesn't argue with them. he takes what they've found and turns it outward: as you are dear to yourself, so others are to themselves.

practice: Notice, without judgment, how much you want to be safe, to be well, to be treated fairly, and let that be fully true.
Then bring to mind someone you'll see today, maybe someone difficult, sitting somewhere with exactly the same wish, just as strong. Hold both at once for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Piya, dear or beloved. King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika agree no one is dearer to them than themselves, and the Buddha turns it into a reason not to harm.

orig.note: Pali piya: dear, beloved. the question is whether anyone is piyatara, dearer, than oneself.

carryVoice: Your line: everyone loves themselves. That's where kindness can quietly start. A full week, done.
